text: OpenStreetMap (OSM), launched in 2004 by Steve Coast in the UK, is a collaborative world map built by volunteers — often called the 'Wikipedia of maps,' it has become the world's most comprehensive open geographic dataset, with over 10 million registered contributors.
The name 'Venezuela' means 'Little Venice' in Spanish — given by explorer Amerigo Vespucci in 1499 after he saw indigenous stilt houses built over Lake Maracaibo, which reminded him of Venice.

Pompeii, buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, is history's most famous abandoned city — rediscovered in 1748, it preserves a uniquely intact snapshot of Roman urban life including bakeries, brothels, temples, and streets complete with wheel ruts.

Lewis and Clark's Corps of Discovery (1804–1806) was the first American overland expedition to the Pacific coast — it mapped roughly 8,000 kilometers of previously uncharted North American territory and encountered over 50 Indigenous nations, dramatically expanding cartographic knowledge of western North America.

Portolan charts, produced primarily in Mediterranean port cities from the 13th to 17th centuries, were among the world's first accurate navigational maps — drawn on vellum (sheepskin) and covered with rhumb line networks called 'wind roses,' they enabled precise coastal navigation.

The name 'Mozambique' is believed to derive from the name of a local Swahili sultan, Mussa al-Big (or Musa ibn Mbiki), whose island Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama encountered in 1498 — making it one of few country names originating from a specific historical person.

Fordlândia, a planned company town built by Henry Ford in the Brazilian Amazon in 1928 to produce rubber, was abandoned in 1934 after crop disease and worker unrest caused total failure — it still stands largely intact as one of the most extraordinary ghost towns in South America.

Nowa Huta, built outside Kraków in communist Poland from 1949, is one of Europe's best-preserved examples of a socialist planned city — designed as a steel-producing workers' utopia with wide boulevards, monumental architecture, and no church (until residents built one after years of struggle).

The Lambert Conformal Conic projection is widely used for aeronautical charts and official government maps of mid-latitude regions because it preserves local shapes (conformality) and makes straight lines approximate great circle routes — the standard projection for US national topographic maps.
The name 'Himalaya' derives from Sanskrit: 'hima' (snow) + 'ālaya' (abode), meaning 'abode of snow' — an apt description of the range that contains all fourteen of Earth's peaks above 8,000 meters.

John Franklin's lost Arctic expedition (1845) sought the Northwest Passage but both ships became icebound — all 129 men perished, and the disaster spurred over 30 rescue missions that collectively mapped most of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago.

The town of Épécuen, Argentina, thrived as a lakeside spa resort until 1985 when floodgates failed and the salt lake rose to bury the entire town under 10 meters of water — when it receded by 2009, ghostly salt-encrusted ruins re-emerged as a surreal tourist attraction.

Shenzhen, China, transformed from a fishing village of 30,000 people in 1979 to a megacity of over 17 million by 2020 after being designated China's first Special Economic Zone — arguably the fastest urban growth of any planned city in history.

The cadastral map — a large-scale map showing ownership boundaries of land parcels — originated in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia and has been essential to property law, taxation, and urban planning for millennia; today GIS-based cadastral systems manage land records for most nations.

The name 'Senegal' is thought to derive from the Wolof phrase 'Sunuu Gaal,' meaning 'our boat' — a possible reference to a misunderstanding between Portuguese explorers in the 15th century and Wolof fishermen they encountered on the river.

Oradour-sur-Glane, France, was massacred by Nazi SS troops in June 1944 and the village was left as it stood — the French government kept the burned ruins as a permanent memorial, making it one of Europe's most haunting preserved ghost villages.

The choropleth map — a thematic map that shades regions according to a statistical variable — was invented by Charles Dupin in 1826 to display literacy rates across French departments, establishing a visualization technique now ubiquitous in GIS and data journalism.

Roald Amundsen's team became the first to reach the South Pole on December 14, 1911, beating Robert Falcon Scott by 33 days — Amundsen's success depended on superior knowledge of polar geography, correct use of sled dogs, and a depot-laying strategy that minimized risk.

The name 'Mozambique Channel' and the country itself may share an origin with the Arabic 'Musa ibn Mbiki,' but 'Madagascar' has a more colorful origin: Marco Polo confused it with the real island of Mogadishu and applied the Italian corruption 'Madagascar' to the wrong island on a map.

Kolkata (formerly Calcutta) was the colonial capital of British India until 1911, when the capital was moved to the purpose-built city of New Delhi — designed by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker with broad ceremonial avenues and grand colonial government buildings.

The 1000th geography fact marks a milestone: the Ordnance Survey of Great Britain, founded in 1791, produced the first detailed national topographic series in the world — the 'one-inch-to-the-mile' map — and pioneered triangulation survey methods that became the global standard for national cartography.

Letoianni and Savoca in Sicily are not ghost towns, but Craco, Roscigno Vecchia, and Pentedattilo are — the latter, a Greek-founded village perched on a jagged rock in Calabria that looks like a giant hand, was abandoned after earthquakes and depopulation, and its name means 'five fingers' in Greek.

The Transverse Mercator projection, developed by Johann Lambert in 1772 and refined for the Gauss-Krüger system, forms the mathematical basis for the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) coordinate system — the global standard grid used by militaries, GPS devices, and most GIS software worldwide.

The name 'Bering Strait' and 'Bering Sea' honor Vitus Bering, the Danish-born Russian explorer who, on his 1741 expedition, became the first European to sight the coast of Alaska — he died of scurvy on the return voyage and is buried on what is now called Bering Island.

Porto Flavia, Sardinia, and Deception Island in Antarctica are both ghost industrial sites: Deception Island hosted a British whaling station from 1906 to 1931 and later scientific stations before volcanic eruptions forced abandonment, leaving behind rusting equipment and whale bones on a ring-shaped volcanic caldera.

Songdo IBD in South Korea is one of the 21st century's most ambitious planned cities — built on 600 hectares of reclaimed land near Incheon from 2003, it was designed entirely around sensors and networked infrastructure, aiming to be a 'smart city' from its foundations.

The name 'Atlantic' derives from Greek mythology's Atlas — the Titan who held up the heavens — and the ocean was called 'Sea of Atlas' by ancient Greeks who believed the god's mountains (the Atlas range in Morocco) were at the ocean's eastern edge.

Eratosthenes of Cyrene (c. 276–194 BCE) calculated Earth's circumference with remarkable accuracy — using the angle of shadows at noon in Alexandria and Syene simultaneously, he estimated 39,375 kilometers, only about 2% off the actual value of 40,075 kilometers.

Wittenoom, Western Australia, was a blue asbestos mining town that operated from 1943 to 1966; declared a public health hazard due to asbestos contamination, it was officially degazetted (removed from maps) by the Australian government in 2007 — one of the few places erased from official cartography.

The word 'Pacific' was coined by Ferdinand Magellan in 1520 when he entered the ocean and found it remarkably calm after the stormy Drake Passage — from the Latin 'mare pacificum,' meaning 'peaceful sea,' a name that persists despite the Pacific hosting more tropical cyclones than any other ocean.

Auroville in Tamil Nadu, India, is a unique international planned township founded in 1968 and conceived by the Indian philosopher Sri Aurobindo's disciple 'The Mother' — it aims to be a universal city outside national politics, with residents from over 50 nations and no official currency within its 'township.'

The Ebstorf Mappa Mundi (c. 1234), the largest medieval world map ever made at 3.6 meters across, was drawn on 30 goatskins and placed Christ's head at the top (east), hands at the sides, and feet at the bottom (west) — integrating Christian cosmology with geographic knowledge before it was destroyed in 1943 during WWII.

The Digital Elevation Model (DEM) — a 3D representation of terrain derived from satellite or aerial data — was first produced for the entire Earth by NASA's Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) in 2000, which mapped 80% of Earth's land surface in just 11 days at 30-meter resolution.
